To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
musicians do not benefit from F0 differences in speech in noise.

(1) Musicians did not benefit from differences of fundamental frequency (F _{0} ) when listening to speech either in a competing two-talker mask or in a background noise; (2) Speech intelligibility increased with increasing F _{0} differences between the target speech and a competing two-talkers masker; and (3) Musicians were significantly better than non-musicians at discriminating F _{0}, but this ability was not correlated with their speech intelligibility scores
musicians did not have an advantage over a group of non-musicians when listening to speech with a monotone fundamental frequency or when the fundamental frequency was varied.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ability to understand speech in noise.
the effects of musical training on the perception of speech.
the question whether musicians are more successful in understanding speech in the presence and absence of interfering speech than non-musicians.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
musical experience does not lead to improved speech understanding in noise.
musicians are not better than non-musicians at understanding speech in noise.

musicians are not better than non-musicians at speech understanding in competing speech backgrounds, and that F0 differences are not an effective cue for target speech segregation in these conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
musical training does not provide a general advantage for speech perception in complex speech backgrounds.
musical training is not associated with improved speech understanding in complex acoustic environments, but that it is associated with better discrimination of fundamental frequency differences.
musicians are not better than non-musicians at understanding speech, but that musicians have better F0 discrimination than non-musician.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the F0 differences between the target and competing talkers are important for speech intelligibility and that the F0 discrimination abilities of the musicians were sufficient to explain the observed F0 intelligibility benefit.
the speech intelligibility advantage of musicians in noise is not related to their ability to use differences in F0 between target and masker.
musicians do not benefit from their superior ability to discriminate differences in fundamental frequency in the context of speech perception.
